text: {{c1::Thales::this thinker}} held that {{c2::water}} is the arche, the first principle of all things
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} of {{c2::Miletus}} is traditionally called the first Greek philosopher
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} held that the earth floats on water, like a log, as Aristotle reports
Herodotus credits {{c1::Thales::this thinker}} with predicting the solar eclipse of 585 BC
The eclipse predicted by {{c1::Thales::this thinker}} halted a battle between the Lydians and the Medes
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} is said to have diverted the Halys River so that Croesus’s army could cross it
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} was counted among the Seven Sages of Greece
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} is said to have brought geometry to Greece after visiting Egypt
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} said that “all things are full of gods”
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} predicted a bumper olive harvest from the stars and cornered the market in olive presses, showing that philosophy can make money
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} fell into a well while gazing at the stars, and a Thracian servant girl laughed at him, in Plato’s *Theaetetus*
Diogenes Laertius credits {{c1::Thales::this thinker}} with the maxim “Know thyself”
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}}’s theorem states that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} is said to have measured the height of the pyramids from their shadows
{{c1::Thales::this thinker}} held that magnets have souls, since they can move iron
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} held that the first principle is the {{c2::apeiron}}, the boundless or indefinite
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} of Miletus was a student and successor of {{c2::Thales}}
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} held that pairs of opposites, such as hot and cold or wet and dry, separate out of the boundless
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}}’s one surviving fragment says that things pay penalty to one another for their injustice, according to the ordering of time
Heidegger wrote an essay on the “saying” of {{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}}
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} wrote the earliest known prose work titled *On Nature*
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} is credited with bringing the gnomon, a kind of sundial, to Greece
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} drew the first map of the world
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} held that the earth is a squat cylinder, like a drum, and we live on its flat top
{{c1::Anaximander::this thinker}} argued that the earth stays at the centre of the cosmos because it has no reason to move in one direction rather than another
{{c1::Anaximenes::this thinker}} held that the first principle is {{c2::air}}
{{c1::Anaximenes::this thinker}} was the third and last thinker of the {{c2::Milesian school}}, and a student of Anaximander
{{c1::Anaximenes::this thinker}} held that air condenses into wind, cloud, water, earth, and stone, and rarefies into fire
{{c1::Anaximenes::this thinker}} held that the earth is a flat disk riding on air
{{c1::Anaximenes::this thinker}} argued that just as our soul, being air, holds us together, breath and air encompass the whole world
